events.supporting_text: The UK devoted approximately 11 per cent of its US$3.9 billion fiscal stimulus to green investments as well as launching a 'Green economy' budget in April 2009, which included a range of low-carbon investments aimed at creating 400,000 new jobs over an eight-year period.

events.title: Adoption of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act
events.description: The United States enacted a US$78.5 billion recovery package in February 2009 that incorporated measures to retrofit buildings, expand mass transit, freight rail, renewable energy and to build a smart electrical‑grid transmission system.
events.supporting_text: In February 2009, the USA adopted a US$78.5 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, which included measures to retrofit buildings and expand mass transit, freight rail and renewable energy as well as construct a 'smart' electrical grid transmission system.

events.title: Publication of "Towards a Green Economy: Pathways to Sustainable Development and Poverty Eradication"
events.description: UNEP released a report in February 2011 advocating green investment worldwide, linking green economies to poverty eradication and outlining investment recommendations across ten key sectors.
events.supporting_text: In February 2011, UNEP published Towards a Green Economy: Pathways to Sustainable Development and Poverty Eradication, which further advocated green investment on a global scale.

events.title: G20 Green Stimulus Spending During the Recession
events.description: Throughout the global recession, G20 members collectively spent over US$520 billion on green stimulus measures, representing 16 % of all fiscal spending and 0.7 % of G20 GDP, though falling short of the 1 % GGND recommendation.
events.supporting_text: During the recession, members of the G20 spent over US$520 billion on a green stimulus. The stimulus comprised 16 per cent of all fiscal spending and 0.7 per cent of the G20 GDP, falling short of the 1 per cent GGND recommendation.

events.title: Publication of *Prosperity Without Growth*
events.description: Tim Jackson’s book argues for a different kind of economy that allows human flourishing within ecological limits, critiquing growth‑driven consumerism and calling for a transition to clean, renewable energy technologies.
events.supporting_text: In Prosperity Without Growth (2009), Tim Jackson argues that a different kind of economy is essential for a different kind of prosperity - one where human beings can flourish within the ecological limits of a finite planet.

events.title: Rio+20 United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development
events.description: The international community’s attention turns to the Rio+20 summit, a high‑level conference that focuses on integrating green‑economy strategies with poverty‑reduction goals.
events.supporting_text: as the international community turns its attention to Rio+20.

events.title: End of food rationing in the United Kingdom
events.description: All food rationing in the UK was terminated, marking the end of wartime and post‑war rationing policies.
events.supporting_text: it was not until July 1954 that all food rationing in the UK came to an end.

events.title: Opening of the Preston by‑pass
events.description: The Preston by‑pass was opened, inaugurating the ‘motorway age’ in Britain.
events.supporting_text: the 'motorway age' was born when the Preston by‑pass was opened in December 1958

events.title: Opening of the M1 motorway
events.description: The M1, the first long stretch of inter‑urban motorway in the UK, was opened, further expanding the national road network.
events.supporting_text: followed in November 1959 by the M1, the first long stretch of inter‑urban motorway.

events.title: Publication of *Unsafe at Any Speed*
events.description: Ralph Nader published a book exposing the automobile industry's resistance to improving vehicle pollution and safety, sparking a new wave of consumer advocacy.
events.supporting_text: In 1965, Ralph Nader (b. 1934) published Unsafe at Any Speed, which examined the reluctance of the car industry to improve both vehicle pollution and safety.

events.title: Launch of ITV, the first independent television station in the UK
events.description: ITV began broadcasting, ending the BBC's monopoly and introducing commercial television advertising to British audiences.
events.supporting_text: Two years later, the BBC's monopoly of television came to an end when the first independent television station, ITV, went on air.

events.title: Coronation of Queen Elizabeth II
events.description: The coronation ceremony of Queen Elizabeth II took place, prompting many British families to purchase their first television sets.
events.supporting_text: In 1953 many families in the UK bought their first television for the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II.

events.title: Publication of "The Affluent Society"
events.description: Economist J. K. Galbraith published his book *The Affluent Society*, identifying the imbalance between newly‑found private wealth and its environmental effects.
events.supporting_text: The economist J. K. Galbraith (1908-2006) eloquently identified the imbalance between the new‑found private wealth and its environmental effects in his book The Affluent Society (1956).

events.title: Cuyahoga River oil slick fire (media coverage)
events.description: Television coverage of the 1969 oil slick fire on the Cuyahoga River highlighted the human impact on the environment and helped raise public awareness of pollution.
events.supporting_text: Coverage of the 1969 oil slick fire on the Cuyahoga River ... were key moments in the growing media coverage of the human impact on the environment.

events.title: Santa Barbara Channel oil spill (media coverage)
events.description: Media reporting on the Santa Barbara Channel oil spill contributed to growing public concern about environmental damage caused by industrial accidents.
events.supporting_text: ... and the Santa Barbara Channel oil spill were key moments in the growing media coverage of the human impact on the environment.

events.title: Capture of the first Earthrise image by Apollo 8 crew
events.description: On Christmas Eve, 24 December 1968, the Apollo 8 crew photographed Earth rising over the lunar landscape, creating the iconic “Earthrise” image that later influenced environmental consciousness.
events.supporting_text: The first pictures of Earth from space were actually taken by the crew of Apollo 8 eight months earlier, on Christmas Eve in December 1968... The first image of Earth rising in the vast darkness of space over a lunar landscape became an iconic picture. ... the image became known as 'Earthrise'.

events.title: Apollo 11 Moon landing
events.description: On 20 July 1969 the US lunar module Eagle landed on the Moon; extensive television coverage and the iconic images of Earth from space helped bring modern environmental concepts into the mainstream.
events.supporting_text: What had been a dream for many people, ... became a reality on 20 July 1969 when the US lunar module Eagle successfully landed on the moon's surface. ... the extensive television coverage of humanity's first mission to land on the moon, and the images of planet Earth from space, also helped to bring modern environmental concepts into the mainstream.

events.title: Proposal of the first Earth Day by Senator Gaylord Nelson
events.description: On 22 April 1970 US Senator Gaylord Nelson proposed the first Earth Day, which was marked by a nationwide teach‑in involving schools, colleges, universities and community groups, and attracted an estimated 20 million participants.
events.supporting_text: A year after the moon landing, US senator Gaylord Nelson (1916-2005) proposed the first Earth Day on 22 April 1970. The day was marked by a national environment teach‑in led by schools, colleges, universities and community groups. Media coverage included a primetime CBS News Special Report called Earth Day: A Question of Survival.

events.title: Broadcast of CBS News Special Report "Earth Day: A Question of Survival"
events.description: A primetime CBS News special report aired during the first Earth Day, focusing on the survival of the planet and highlighting environmental challenges.
events.supporting_text: Media coverage included a primetime CBS News Special Report called Earth Day: A Question of Survival.

events.title: Founding of Keep America Beautiful
events.description: Keep America Beautiful (KAB) was founded by a group of US corporate and civic leaders to promote and develop a national cleanliness ethic in response to the growing problem of litter.
events.supporting_text: KAB was founded in 1953 by a group of US corporate and civic leaders to promote and develop a national cleanliness ethic in response to the growing problem of litter.

events.title: First public service announcement on litter prevention by Keep America Beautiful
events.description: Keep America Beautiful produced its first public service announcement aimed at preventing litter.
events.supporting_text: in 1956 it produced its first public service announcement on litter prevention.

events.title: Earth Day campaign (1970)
events.description: The Earth Day campaign highlighted the need for individuals and communities to protect the environment.
events.supporting_text: By 1970, the Earth Day campaign was again highlighting the need for individuals and communities to do their bit to protect the environment.

events.title: Launch of the 'Crying Indian' public announcement campaign
events.description: Keep America Beautiful launched the iconic 'Crying Indian' TV advert to promote personal environmental responsibility.
events.supporting_text: In 1971, Keep America Beautiful (KAB) launched the 'Crying Indian' public announcement campaign, which was to become an iconic symbol of personal environmental responsibility.

events.title: Adoption of Oregon Bottle Bill
events.description: The State of Oregon passed a landmark Bottle Bill requiring a five‑cent deposit on beer and soft‑drink containers to reduce litter and conserve resources.
events.supporting_text: in 1971 the State of Oregon's landmark Bottle Bill became law in spite of intense lobbying by container and beverage industries.

events.title: Proposal of California Bottle Bill
events.description: The State of California proposed a bottle‑deposit bill similar to Oregon’s, which faced public opposition from Keep America Beautiful.
events.supporting_text: In 1974, the State of California proposed a similar bill but KAB publicly opposed it

events.title: Launch of Clean Community System
events.description: Keep America Beautiful introduced the Clean Community System, emphasizing street cleaning and other litter‑control activities as an alternative to bottle‑deposit legislation.
events.supporting_text: and a year later launched the Clean Community System as an alternative that placed an emphasis on street cleaning and other litter-control activities.

events.title: Materials recovery program launched in Woodbury, New Jersey
events.description: Woodbury became the first U.S. city to begin a materials‑recovery (recycling) program, led by a local community organization.
events.supporting_text: In November 1970, Woodbury, New Jersey was the first US city to begin materials recovery, spearheaded by an environmentally concerned community organisation.

events.title: Ecology Center recycling demonstration project in Berkeley
events.description: The Ecology Center launched a newspaper‑collection recycling demonstration in Berkeley, which served as a model for municipal recycling programmes.
events.supporting_text: In 1973, the Ecology Center, a US action-orientated organisation, launched a recycling demonstration project in Berkeley, California collecting newspapers, which became a model for other municipal recycling programmes.

events.title: Installation of UK's first bottle bank at Tesco, Barnsley
events.description: The UK's first bottle bank was installed in the car park of a Tesco supermarket in Barnsley, South Yorkshire, introduced by Stanley Race to promote glass recycling.
events.supporting_text: In August 1977, the UK's first bottle bank was sited in the car park of the Tesco supermarket in Barnsley, South Yorkshire. The bottle bank was introduced by Stanley Race, then president of the Glass Manufacturers' Federation, with the aim of convincing local authorities that such schemes could be environmentally friendly and pay for themselves.

events.title: 1973 OPEC oil export embargo
events.description: Major Arab oil‑producing states imposed an oil export embargo through OPEC, causing a hike in oil prices and an oil crisis that spurred national debates on energy security in the UK.
actors: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC)
events.supporting_text: In 1973, an oil export embargo of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) by major Arab oil-producing states caused a hike in the price of oil, leading an oil crisis.

events.title: Publication of The Aerosol Connection pamphlet
events.description: Friends of the Earth (FoE) in the UK published a pamphlet titled “The Aerosol Connection” listing CFC‑free aerosols and launching a publicity campaign encouraging consumers to choose them.
events.supporting_text: In 1986, the UK FoE published a pamphlet, The Aerosol Connection, detailing a list of aerosols that were CFC‑free.

events.title: Launch of FoE aerosol boycott campaign
events.description: Friends of the Earth planned to boycott best‑selling CFC‑based aerosols; the boycott was launched three days after the eight largest aerosol companies decided to phase out all CFCs by the end of 1989.
events.supporting_text: When this approach failed to persuade aerosol manufacturers to take action, FoE planned to boycott all the best‑selling CFC‑based aerosols. The eight largest aerosol companies took the decision to phase out all CFCs by the end of 1989, three days before the boycott campaign was launched.

events.title: Publication of The Green Consumer Guide
events.description: John Elkington and Julia Hailes co‑authored and published “The Green Consumer Guide”, the first book focusing on green consumer choices, selling over one million copies.
events.supporting_text: In 1988, John Elkington (b. 1949) and Julia Hailes (b. 1961) published The Green Consumer Guide, which reflected the growing interest in green consumerism and further encouraged individuals who wanted to use their purchasing power to buy the greenest products.

events.title: Launch of six new British ethical investment funds
events.description: A boom in ethical investment in the late 1980s led to the creation and launch of six new ethical funds in Britain.
events.supporting_text: In 1987 a boom in ethical investment saw the launch of six new British ethical funds.

events.title: 1989 American survey on environmental concerns of product purchases
events.description: A survey of Americans found that 89 % were concerned about the environmental impacts of the products they bought and 77 % were influenced by a company's environmental reputation.
events.supporting_text: A 1989 survey of Americans found that 89 per cent were concerned about the environmental impacts of the products they bought, while 77 per cent were influenced by a company's environmental reputation.

events.title: Organised consumer action against McDonald's
events.description: US environmental groups EDF, Earth Action Network and Kids Against Pollution launched a campaign targeting McDonald's over its waste, using tactics such as sending back wrappers and schoolchildren demonstrations.
events.supporting_text: In 1988, the US environmental groups EDF, Earth Action Network and Kids Against Pollution attacked McDonald's, the largest US fast-food chain, for the amount of rubbish it produced.

events.title: McDonald's adoption of paper‑based packaging
events.description: Following pressure on its non‑recyclable waste, McDonald's agreed to replace polystyrene clamshells with paper‑based packaging.
events.supporting_text: the company was subjected to mounting pressure on its nonrecyclable waste and in 1990 agreed to move to paper-based packaging.

events.title: Founding of The Body Shop
events.description: Anita Roddick established The Body Shop in Brighton, UK, to sell natural beauty products and promote environmentally conscious consumerism.
events.supporting_text: In 1976, Anita Roddick (1942-2007) founded The Body Shop in Brighton, UK to sell natural beauty products.

events.title: Launch of 'Save the Whale' window campaign by The Body Shop
events.description: The Body Shop, in collaboration with Greenpeace, created a window display campaign titled 'Save the Whale' to raise awareness of marine conservation.
events.supporting_text: In 1986 it created its own window campaign, 'Save the whale', in collaboration with Greenpeace.

events.title: Gallup poll on executive attitudes toward recyclable packaging
events.description: A Gallup poll revealed that 58 % of Fortune 500 executives believed customers would pay more for products with recyclable packaging or components.
events.supporting_text: A 1989 Gallup poll found that 58 per cent of Fortune magazine's 500 list of business executives believed their customers would pay more for products with recyclable packaging or components.

events.title: Survey on consumer skepticism toward environmental claims
events.description: A 1990 survey indicated that 47 % of customers dismissed environmental claims as mere 'gimmickry', reflecting growing consumer wariness of greenwashing.
events.supporting_text: One 1990 survey indicated that 47 per cent of customers dismissed environmental claims as mere 'gimmickry'.

events.title: Introduction of the EU voluntary Ecolabel scheme
events.description: The European Union launched a voluntary Ecolabel scheme to help consumers identify green products and encourage businesses to advertise environmental credentials.
events.supporting_text: One way of addressing this was through labelling, and the EU introduced a voluntary Ecolabel scheme in 1992.

events.title: Awarding of over 1,000 EU Ecolabel licences
events.description: By early 2010 more than 1,000 licences under the EU Ecolabel had been granted, with Italy and France holding the highest numbers of licence holders.
events.supporting_text: At the beginning of 2010, more than 1000 EU Ecolabel licences had been awarded, with Italy and France having the highest number of Ecolabel holders.

events.title: Tesco announcement of product carbon‑footprint labelling and emissions cut
events.description: Tesco announced it would label 70,000 products with carbon‑footprint information and aim to cut store carbon emissions by 75 %.
events.supporting_text: In 2007, Britain's leading businesses responded to a resurging green trend, with the supermarket chain Tesco announcing it would be labelling 70,000 products with details of its carbon footprint, and that it would cut carbon emissions from its stores by 75 per cent.

events.title: Marks & Spencer launch of 'Plan A' programme
events.description: Marks & Spencer launched a £200 million 'Plan A' programme aimed at making the company carbon neutral through energy reduction and increased use of recycled materials.
events.supporting_text: Marks & Spencer launched a £200 million 'Plan A' programme to make the company carbon neutral by cutting energy consumption and stocking more products from recycled materials.

events.title: Broadcast of "The Undersea World of Jacques Cousteau"
events.description: US broadcast of the television series that brought marine life to public attention for the first time.
events.supporting_text: The 1966 US broadcast of The Undersea World of Jacques Cousteau brought life under the seas to public attention for the very first time.

events.title: Release of documentary "Life on Earth"
events.description: David Attenborough produced a highly acclaimed documentary that narrated the evolution of life on the planet.
events.supporting_text: In 1979, Attenborough produced a highly acclaimed documentary, Life on Earth, which told the story of the evolution of life on the planet.

events.title: Earth Day celebration at Union Square
events.description: Actors Paul Newman and Ali McGraw participated in the 1970 Earth Day celebration in New York City.
locations: Union Square, New York City, USA
events.supporting_text: US actors Paul Newman (1925-2008) and Ali McGraw (b. 1939) took part in the 1970 Earth Day celebration at Union Square in New York City.

events.title: Live Aid concert
events.description: International artists performed at Live Aid on 13 July 1985, raising money for the Ethiopian famine and demonstrating the power of celebrity endorsement for environmentalists.
events.supporting_text: the success of the Live Aid concert on 13 July 1985 which galvanised a host of international artists to raise money to tackle the Ethiopian famine, that environmentalists realised the power of celebrity endorsement.

events.title: Founding of Rainforest Foundation International
events.description: British musician Sting, his wife Trudie Styler, and filmmaker Jean‑Pierre Dutilleux established the Rainforest Foundation International.
events.supporting_text: In 1989, British musician Sting (b. 1951) founded the Rainforest Foundation International with his wife Trudie Styler (b. 1954) and Belgian film-maker Jean-Pierre Dutilleux.

events.title: Legal recognition and demarcation of Kayapo territory
events.description: Following a campaign led by Sting and Kayapo leader Raoni Metuktire, the Brazilian government legally recognized and demarcated more than 27,359 km² of indigenous land in Amazonas.
events.supporting_text: In 1993 this resulted in legal recognition and demarcation of an area of more than 27,359 square kilometres.

events.title: Publication of Vanity Fair’s “Green Issue”
events.description: Vanity Fair released a special “Green Issue” featuring Julia Roberts, George Clooney, Al Gore and Robert Kennedy Jr., calling for a new American revolution on climate change.
events.supporting_text: In May 2006, US Vanity Fair, a magazine of popular culture, fashion and politics, reflected popular environmental awareness when it published its 'Green Issue'. The cover featured Hollywood movie stars Julia Roberts (b. 1967) and George Clooney (b. 1961), and politicians Al Gore (b. 1948) and Robert Kennedy Jr (b. 1954), dressed in complementary shades of green.

events.title: Vanity Fair abandons annual Green Issue
events.description: Three years after the Green Issue launch, Vanity Fair announced it would cease publishing the annual green issue, stating that environmental coverage had become integral to the news agenda.
events.supporting_text: Three years later, Vanity Fair announced it would abandon its annual green issue, arguing that the environment had become so integral to the news agenda that there was no longer a need for a dedicated issue.

events.title: Release of documentary "An Inconvenient Truth"
events.description: Al Gore produced the Oscar‑winning documentary that presented the scientific case for climate change and its impacts.
events.supporting_text: In 2006, former US Democratic Party Vice President Al Gore's long-standing interest in environmental issues led him to produce the Oscar-winning documentary An Inconvenient Truth.

events.title: Release of film "The Day After Tomorrow"
events.description: Hollywood science‑fiction disaster film depicting catastrophic climate‑change scenarios.
events.supporting_text: This followed the 2004 Hollywood science-fiction disaster film The Day After Tomorrow.

events.title: Release of documentary "The 11th Hour"
events.description: Leonardo DiCaprio produced and narrated a feature documentary on the state of the natural environment.
events.supporting_text: In 2007, US actor Leonardo DiCaprio (b. 1974) produced and narrated the feature film documentary The 11th Hour on the state of the natural environment.

events.title: Release of film "The Age of Stupid"
events.description: Franny Armstrong produced a drama‑documentary‑animation hybrid about climate change, starring Pete Postlethwaite.
events.supporting_text: In 2009 British environmental campaigner Franny Armstrong (b. 1972) produced the film The Age of Stupid, which continued the climate change theme.

events.title: Live Earth concert 2007
events.description: A global series of concerts calling for worldwide action to combat climate change, staged on seven continents and broadcast in 132 countries.
events.supporting_text: The 2007 Live Earth concert called for worldwide action to combat climate change across seven continents, and was broadcast in 132 countries. Described as the 'largest global entertainment event in history', Live Earth staged concerts in New York, London, Sydney, Tokyo, Shanghai, Rio de Janeiro, Johannesburg and Hamburg - as well as special broadcast events in Antarctica, Kyoto and Washington, DC.

events.title: Publication of Climate Safety report
events.description: Report by the Public Interest Research Centre concluding the need for a 10 % reduction in the developed world's emissions by the end of 2010.
events.supporting_text: In 2008, the Public Interest Research Centre's report Climate Safety concluded the need for a 10 per cent reduction in the developed world's emissions by the end of 2010.

events.title: Founding of the 10:10 campaign
events.description: Campaign encouraging individuals, businesses and organisations to commit to reducing their carbon emissions, founded by filmmaker Franny Armstrong.
events.supporting_text: This inspired Armstrong to found the 10:10 campaign, which encouraged individuals, businesses and organisations to commit to reducing their carbon emissions.

events.title: Establishment of Active Resistance project
events.description: Project set up by designer Vivienne Westwood to encourage engagement with humanitarian and environmental issues.
events.supporting_text: In 2005, the designer Vivenne Westwood (b. 1941) set up 'Active Resistance' as a project to encourage engagement with humanitarian and environmental issues.

events.title: Launch of 'I am not a plastic bag' cotton bag
events.description: An unbleached £5 cotton bag designed by Anya Hindmarch for Sainsbury's, bearing the slogan 'I am not a plastic bag', which sold out within an hour.
events.supporting_text: In 2007, bag designer Anya Hindmarch (b.1968) designed an unbleached £5 cotton bag with 'I am not a plastic bag' written on it for Sainsbury's supermarket.

events.title: Conversion of Duchy Home Farm to organic agriculture
events.description: Process begun by Prince Charles in the early 1980s to convert the Duchy Home Farm on the Highgrove estate to an organic agricultural system.
events.supporting_text: In the early 1980s, when Prince Charles moved to the Highgrove estate in Gloucestershire, he began the process of converting the Duchy Home Farm, which is part of the estate, to an organic agricultural system.

events.title: Launch of Duchy Originals organic brand
events.description: Prince Charles launched his own organic brand, Duchy Originals, to produce natural, organic products and support countryside and wildlife protection.
events.supporting_text: In 1990, he launched his own organic brand, Duchy Originals, which embodies the Prince of Wales's commitment to producing natural, organic products while helping to protect and sustain the countryside and wildlife.

events.title: Setting of household carbon emissions reduction target
events.description: Prince Charles's household set a target to reduce its carbon emissions by 25 % by 2012, using 2007 as the baseline year.
events.supporting_text: In 2007, his household set a target to reduce its carbon emissions by 25 per cent by 2012 against a baseline year of 2007.

events.title: Prince Charles speech to the European Parliament
events.description: First speech by Prince Charles to the European Parliament, calling for EU leadership in the war against climate change.
events.supporting_text: Following this, in his first speech to the European Parliament on 14 February 2008, the Prince called for EU leadership in the war against climate change.

events.title: Prince Charles BBC lecture on climate change
events.description: BBC lecture where Prince Charles argued that people must change their behaviour to stop the effects of climate change.
events.supporting_text: He also used a 2009 BBC lecture to argue that it is essential that people change their behaviour to stop the effects of climate change.

events.title: Royal Train ecotour and sustainability festival
events.description: Prince Charles undertook a bio‑fuel‑powered Royal Train ecotour across the UK to promote sustainable living, culminating in a sustainability festival attended by about 70,000 people.
events.supporting_text: The Prince's activities continued in 2010, when he undertook an ecotour of the UK in a bio-fuel-powered Royal Train to promote an initiative to encourage and celebrate sustainable living. At the end of the tour, he held a sustainability festival attended by an estimated 70,000 people and demonstrated how everyone could make a difference.

events.title: First Earth Day
events.description: In the USA, public concern for the environment first peaked around the first Earth Day in 1970 and then declined over the following decade.
events.supporting_text: In the USA, public concern for the environment first peaked around the first Earth Day in 1970 and then declined over the following decade.

events.title: Time magazine declares “Endangered Earth” Planet of the Year
events.description: In 1989, the US Time magazine declared “Endangered Earth” as the “Planet of the Year” instead of its usual man or woman of the year.
events.supporting_text: In 1989, the US Time magazine declared 'Endangered Earth' as the 'Planet of the Year' instead of its usual man or woman of the year.

events.title: Environment ranked fourth on national priorities list
events.description: The environment ranked fourth on a 1990 list of national priorities.
events.supporting_text: The environment ranked fourth on a 1990 list of national priorities.

events.title: Climategate controversy
events.description: The November 2009 “climategate” controversy over climate science contributed to a decline in public concern about climate change.
events.supporting_text: The November 2009 'climategate' controversy over climate science (see Chapter 4) contributed to a decline in public concern about climate change.

events.title: 2010 public attitudes survey in England
events.description: A 2010 survey of public attitudes in England revealed that the majority of the public still believed that the climate is changing and were prepared to take action.
events.supporting_text: A 2010 survey of public attitudes in England revealed that the majority of the public still believed that the climate is changing and were prepared to take action.

events.title: Increase in environmental concern during the 1980s
events.description: The 1980s saw an increase in environmental concern with the discovery of climate change, the ozone hole and an increase in environmental disasters such as the Union Carbide gas tragedy in India, the Chernobyl nuclear disaster and the Exxon Valdez oil spill.
events.supporting_text: The 1980s saw an increase in environmental concern with the discovery of climate change, the ozone hole and an increase in environmental disasters such as the Union Carbide gas tragedy in India, the Chernobyl nuclear disaster and the Exxon Valdez oil spill.

events.title: Rapid growth of US public concern for the environment (1987‑1990)
events.description: US public concern for the environment grew much more quickly than any other issue in the period 1987‑90.
events.supporting_text: US public concern for the environment grew much more quickly than any other issue in the period 1987-90.

events.title: 2009 EU study on European public attitudes to climate change
events.description: A European Union‑commissioned survey that found two‑thirds of Europeans considered climate change a very serious problem, while highlighting gaps in knowledge in several member states.
events.supporting_text: A 2009 EU study found that two‑thirds of Europeans felt the climate is a very serious problem. In Turkey, Romania, Bulgaria and Lithuania, citizens felt they were not well informed about the causes and effects of climate change.

events.title: 2010 Yale University study of US public attitudes to climate change
events.description: A Yale University survey that reported 63 % of Americans believed global warming is happening, identified knowledge gaps and misconceptions, and measured trust in scientists and desire for more education on climate change.
events.supporting_text: A 2010 Yale University study of US public attitudes to climate change found that 63 per cent of Americans believed that global warming is happening. The study also found gaps in knowledge and common misconceptions about climate change.

events.title: Publication of "Sizzle: The New Climate Message" report
events.description: A report by the sustainability communications consultancy Futerra that argues campaigns should focus on a positive, appealing vision of a greener life to re‑engage the public and media.
events.supporting_text: A report by the sustainability communications consultancy Futerra, Sizzle: The New Climate Message, argues that in order to reinvigorate public and media interest, campaigns need to focus on a vision of a greener life that is positive and appealing to all.

events.title: 2009 UK survey on green lifestyle attitudes
events.description: A national survey that revealed public confusion about what constitutes a green lifestyle, showing mixed attitudes toward personal environmental impact and guilt about harmful behaviours.
events.supporting_text: This confusion about what a green lifestyle actually entails is evident in the responses to a 2009 UK survey on the issue.

events.title: Development of environmentalism within popular culture
events.description: A multi‑decadal process, beginning in the 1960s, through which environmentalism entered mainstream Western culture, acquiring a counter‑cultural element and influencing media, consumerism, and celebrity discourse.
events.supporting_text: This chapter has examined how environmentalism developed as part of popular culture over the past sixty years. In the 1960s, environmental issues burst into the public consciousness with unprecedented speed and urgency.

actors.role: Creates and disseminates climate assessment reports that serve as the scientific basis for policy and governance actions on climate change.
actors.supporting_text: When the IPCC was created, its purpose was to make climate science relevant, understandable and clear.

actors.name: Global Climate Coalition
actors.description: An American industrial grouping formed in the early 1990s to represent the interests of fossil‑fuel and related industries.
actors.role: Challenged the scientific certainty presented in IPCC publications and opposed policy measures aimed at reducing greenhouse‑gas emissions.
actors.supporting_text: For much of the 1990s, the Global Climate Coalition, an American industrial grouping formed shortly after the IPCC, challenged the levels of scientific certainty set out in IPCC publications.

actors.name: Wall Street Journal
actors.description: U.S. newspaper that reported on alleged procedural violations in IPCC reports.
actors.role: Published claims that editorial changes to an IPCC report violated its rules, thereby amplifying challenges to the panel’s credibility.
actors.supporting_text: In 1995 the Wall Street Journal picked up and published claims that editorial changes to the second report on the science of climate change were in violation of IPCC rules of procedure and would 'deceive policy makers and the public into believing that the scientific evidence shows human activities are causing global warming'.

actors.name: Fred Singer
actors.description: American physicist and academic known for climate‑skeptic positions.
actors.role: Added scientific authority to a stream of challenges against mainstream climate science and the IPCC’s conclusions.
actors.supporting_text: Academics such as the American physicist Fred Singer (b. 1924) and the Danish statistician Bjørn Lomborg (b. 1965) added scientific authority to a continuous stream of challenges to climate science.

actors.name: Bjørn Lomborg
actors.description: Danish statistician and author who questions the cost‑effectiveness of many climate policies.
actors.role: Provided academic support for critiques of climate‑science consensus and IPCC findings.
actors.supporting_text: Academics such as the American physicist Fred Singer (b. 1924) and the Danish statistician Bjørn Lomborg (b. 1965) added scientific authority to a continuous stream of challenges to climate science.

actors.name: Exxon Mobil
actors.description: Multinational oil and gas corporation, the world’s largest publicly traded energy company.
actors.role: As a member of the Global Climate Coalition, it was publicly challenged by the Royal Society over its stance on climate science.
actors.supporting_text: Direct conflict broke out in 2006 when Exxon Mobil, the world's richest company and a member of the Global Climate Coalition, was challenged in an exchange of letters that became public with the Royal Society, the world's oldest scientific academy.

actors.name: Royal Society
actors.description: The United Kingdom’s national academy of sciences, the world’s oldest scientific academy.
actors.role: Engaged in a public exchange of letters with Exxon Mobil, defending the integrity of climate science and the IPCC process.
actors.supporting_text: Direct conflict broke out in 2006 when Exxon Mobil, the world's richest company and a member of the Global Climate Coalition, was challenged in an exchange of letters that became public with the Royal Society, the world's oldest scientific academy.

actors.name: Climatic Research Unit (CRU)
actors.description: Research unit at the University of East Anglia that compiles global temperature records.
actors.role: Produced key temperature datasets used in IPCC assessments; its email correspondence was hacked, leading to public controversy and scrutiny of climate‑science practices.
actors.supporting_text: The challenge to climate science reached a new peak after approximately 1000 emails from the Climatic Research Unit (CRU) at the University of East Anglia (UEA) were hacked and posted on the internet in November 2009.

actors.name: University of East Anglia (UEA)
actors.description: British university that houses the Climatic Research Unit.
actors.role: Commissioned two independent reviews into the science and conduct of CRU following the email leak.
actors.supporting_text: three independent reviews were commissioned: two by UEA into the science undertaken by CRU and the conduct of scientists involved, and one by the British government.

actors.name: British government
actors.description: The United Kingdom’s central government.
actors.role: Commissioned an independent review of the CRU and later a review of the IPCC after the email controversy.
actors.supporting_text: three independent reviews were commissioned: two by UEA into the science undertaken by CRU and the conduct of scientists involved, and one by the British government.

actors.name: Daily Telegraph
actors.description: The United Kingdom’s most widely circulated broadsheet newspaper.
actors.role: Reported on the hostile climate‑science environment, shaping public perception of scientists during the controversy.
actors.supporting_text: the Daily Telegraph, the most widely circulated broadsheet in the UK, summarised the atmosphere of hostility, claiming nobody was listening to scientists any more and describing them as 'white-coated prima donnas and narcissists [...] pointy heads in lab coats [who] have reassumed the role of mad cranks'.

actors.name: IPCC
actors.description: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the leading global body for assessing climate science.
actors.role: Faces dilemmas in communicating climate science to the public and protecting scientists from political controversy.
actors.supporting_text: How the science of climate change can be communicated to a public audience without being misinterpreted or biased by political arguments is one of the major dilemmas facing the IPCC today.

actors.name: Royal Society
actors.description: The United Kingdom's national academy of sciences, a learned society promoting scientific excellence.
actors.role: Attempted to produce a plain‑English guide to climate change but was forced to alter its wording after internal complaints, illustrating challenges in science communication.
actors.supporting_text: when the Royal Society attempted to write a plain English guide to climate change, it was forced to change its wording following complaints by some of its own members.

actors.name: E. O. Wilson
actors.description: Renowned American biologist and naturalist, author of influential works on biodiversity and sociobiology.
actors.role: Provides a scholarly perspective on how new scientific ideas face resistance before gaining acceptance.
actors.supporting_text: The biologist E. O. Wilson (b. 1929) has observed that 'any new idea will take some serious hits', but that if sound, ideas will ultimately survive.

actors.name: IPCC lead authors
actors.description: Designated scientists responsible for drafting and explaining IPCC assessment reports.
actors.role: Their limited engagement with popular media has diluted the voice of scientists in public climate debates.
actors.supporting_text: the absence of IPCC lead authors explaining their findings under IPCC auspices through popular media has diluted the voice of scientists in the public debate.

actors.name: Adam Smith
actors.description: Scottish economist and author of *The Wealth of Nations*; foundational figure in classical economics.
actors.role: Highlighted rent from land as a primary source of public revenue, emphasizing the economic importance of natural resources in national wealth.
actors.supporting_text: In The Wealth of Nations Adam Smith (1723-90) described rent from the use of land, the wages of labour and profits of stock as 'the three original sources of all revenue as well as of all exchangeable value.'

actors.name: David Ricardo
actors.description: British political economist known for the theory of comparative advantage and contributions to classical economics.
actors.role: Shifted economic focus toward wage labour and capital stock, contributing to the marginalisation of land as a factor of production in later economic thought.
actors.supporting_text: as political economists David Ricardo (1772-1823) and, later, Karl Marx (1818-83) set out their work on economics.

actors.name: Karl Marx
actors.description: German philosopher, economist, and revolutionary socialist; author of *Das Kapital*.
actors.role: Described land as a 'reservoir' of resources, 'powers of nature' and an 'element of production', linking natural resources to industrial and agricultural processes.
actors.supporting_text: Karl Marx described land as providing a 'reservoir' of resources for coal and minerals, as 'powers of nature' driving mills, and as the 'element of production' for agriculture.

actors.name: Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot
actors.description: French economist and statesman, early proponent of the law of diminishing returns in agriculture.
actors.role: Outlined a law of diminishing returns in agriculture, arguing that land productivity has a maximum limit, thereby linking land availability to population and wealth constraints.
actors.supporting_text: Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot (1727-81) outlined a law of diminishing returns in agriculture, arguing that there was a maximum point of land productivity that was impossible to surpass.

actors.name: Thomas Malthus
actors.description: British scholar and demographer, author of *An Essay on the Principle of Population*.
actors.role: Argued that population growth would be limited by finite land and food supplies, framing early concerns about environmental limits to human wellbeing.
actors.supporting_text: an idea forcefully argued by Thomas Malthus (1766-1834) in An Essay on the Principle of Population, as it Affects the Future Improvement of Society (1798), Malthus explained that population growth, driven initially by surplus food production, would eventually be constrained by limits to productive land and a resultant shortage of food.

actors.name: William Stanley Jevons
actors.description: British economist and logician, early analyst of resource depletion.
actors.role: Warned that improvements in fuel efficiency could paradoxically increase total fuel consumption, an early articulation of the rebound effect in environmental economics.
actors.supporting_text: In 1865, William Stanley Jevons (1835-82) published The Coal Question: An Inquiry Concerning the Progress of the Nation, and the Probable Exhaustion of our Coal-mines, in which he argued that improvements in fuel efficiency tended to increase, rather than decrease, fuel use: 'It is a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth.'

actors.name: John Stuart Mill
actors.description: British philosopher, political economist, and civil servant.
actors.role: Championed the concept of a stationary state economy and warned against unlimited economic growth, highlighting the ecological costs of relentless industrial expansion.
actors.supporting_text: John Stuart Mill (1806-73) was among the first economists to treat the environment as more than a unit of land or a means of production. In 1862, he published the Principles of Political Economy with some of their Applications to Social Philosophy, in which he championed the 'stationary state economy' and warned against the drive for unlimited economic growth.

actors.name: Arthur C. Pigou
actors.description: British economist known for work on welfare economics and externalities.
actors.role: Introduced the concept of negative externalities and argued for government intervention when environmental harms are unrecognised, a cornerstone of modern environmental economics.
actors.supporting_text: Later economist Arthur C. Pigou (1877-1959) argued that when the detrimental effects of an activity went unrecognised, then the government should intervene.

actors.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
actors.description: International financial institution established to ensure post‑war peace and prosperity through economic cooperation.
actors.role: Created at the Bretton Woods conference to shape global economic governance, influencing policies that affect environmental and nature‑related outcomes.
actors.supporting_text: The meeting led to the establishment of the IMF and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (now the World Bank).

actors.name: World Bank (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development)
actors.description: International development bank founded to provide financial and technical assistance for reconstruction and development.
actors.role: Formed at Bretton Woods to guide economic reconstruction, its lending and policy advice impact resource use and environmental sustainability.
actors.supporting_text: The meeting led to the establishment of the IMF and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (now the World Bank).

actors.name: Harry S. Truman
actors.description: President of the United States (1945‑1953).
actors.role: Established a presidential commission in 1951 to examine future supplies of minerals, energy and agricultural resources, linking economic growth to natural‑resource planning.
actors.supporting_text: As early as 1951, President Harry S. Truman (1884-1972) established a presidential commission to examine the future supply of minerals, energy and agricultural resources.

actors.name: William Paley
actors.description: Chair of the Paley Commission, author of a five‑volume resource report.
actors.role: Led the Paley Commission that produced "Resources for Freedom: Foundations for Growth and Security," highlighting unprecedented natural‑resource use and its economic implications.
actors.supporting_text: The following year the Paley Commission, chaired by William Paley (1901-90), produced a five-volume report: Resources for Freedom: Foundations for Growth and Security.

actors.name: Paley Commission
actors.description: Presidentially appointed commission chaired by William Paley that studied resource availability.
actors.role: Generated a comprehensive report on mineral, energy and agricultural resource trends, informing U.S. policy on resource planning and economic growth.
actors.supporting_text: The following year the Paley Commission, chaired by William Paley (1901-90), produced a five-volume report: Resources for Freedom: Foundations for Growth and Security.

actors.name: Henry Fairfield Osborn Jr.
actors.description: Conservationist and author of the 1948 book "Our Plundered Planet."
actors.role: Contributed early environmental literature that warned of resource depletion, influencing public discourse on nature’s wellbeing.
actors.supporting_text: These included Henry Fairfield Osborn Jr's (1887-1969) Our Plundered Planet and William Vogt's (1902-68) Road to Survival, both published in 1948.

actors.name: William Vogt
actors.description: Ecologist and author of the 1948 book "Road to Survival."
actors.role: Provided early warnings about overpopulation and environmental limits, shaping the emerging environmental movement.
actors.supporting_text: These included Henry Fairfield Osborn Jr's (1887-1969) Our Plundered Planet and William Vogt's (1902-68) Road to Survival, both published in 1948.

actors.name: David Brower
actors.description: Executive Director of the Sierra Club (1912‑2000).
actors.role: Suggested that biologist Paul R. Ehrlich write a book linking population growth to the environmental movement, thereby mobilising the conservation community.
actors.supporting_text: Over a decade later, David Brower (1912-2000), Executive Director of the Sierra Club, suggested to biologist Paul R. Ehrlich (b. 1932) that he summarise in book form the argument that the population issue should be addressed by the environmental movement.

actors.name: Sierra Club
actors.description: Major U.S. environmental non‑governmental organization.
actors.role: Through its leadership (e.g., David Brower) and advocacy, the club helped bring population and resource issues into the environmental agenda.
actors.supporting_text: Over a decade later, David Brower (1912-2000), Executive Director of the Sierra Club, suggested to biologist Paul R. Ehrlich (b. 1932) that he summarise in book form the argument that the population issue should be addressed by the environmental movement.

actors.name: Paul R. Ehrlich
actors.description: Biologist and author of "The Population Bomb" (1968).
actors.role: Popularised concerns about rapid human population growth and its impact on planetary limits, influencing environmental policy debates.
actors.supporting_text: Over a decade later, David Brower (1912-2000), Executive Director of the Sierra Club, suggested to biologist Paul R. Ehrlich (b. 1932) that he summarise in book form the argument that the population issue should be addressed by the environmental movement.

actors.name: Richard Nixon
actors.description: President of the United States (1969‑1974).
actors.role: Delivered a special message to Congress in 1969 highlighting the problems of population growth, linking demographic trends to national policy considerations.
actors.supporting_text: Concern over the rate of population growth was already reaching high levels when, in 1969, US President Richard Nixon (1913-94) gave a special message to Congress on 'the problems of population growth'.

actors.name: Kenneth E. Boulding
actors.description: Economist and author of the 1966 essay "The Economics of the Coming Spaceship Earth".
actors.role: Challenged the notion of unlimited economic growth by proposing a closed‑economy model that respects planetary resource limits.
actors.supporting_text: In his 1966 essay 'The Economics of the Coming Spaceship Earth', Kenneth E. Boulding (1910-93) challenged neoclassical economic ideas of an 'open' economic system without finite resources and a limited assimilative capacity to absorb waste.

actors.name: John Kenneth Galbraith
actors.description: American economist and author of "The Affluent Society" (1958).
actors.role: Critiqued the post‑war focus on production as the primary measure of progress, raising early questions about the sustainability of growth‑centric economies.
actors.supporting_text: In The Affluent Society (1958), the American economist John Kenneth Galbraith (1908-2006), reflecting on the continued focus on production as a measure of progress, observed:

actors.name: Ehrlich
actors.description: Prominent critic of the focus on economic growth as a measure of progress; co‑author of debates on environmental impacts.
actors.role: Provided scholarly criticism of growth‑centric metrics and co‑developed the IPAT equation to highlight multiple determinants of environmental impact.
actors.supporting_text: Ehrlich and Barry Commoner (b. 1917) became two of the most prominent critics of the focus on economic growth as a measure of progress.

actors.name: Barry Commoner
actors.description: Environmental scholar known for critiquing economic growth and author of *The Closing Circle*.
actors.role: Served as a leading voice opposing growth‑centric policies and engaged in scholarly debate over technology, population, and affluence.
actors.supporting_text: Ehrlich and Barry Commoner (b. 1917) became two of the most prominent critics of the focus on economic growth as a measure of progress.

actors.name: John P. Holdren
actors.description: Scientist and colleague of Ehrlich who engaged in critique of Commoner's emphasis on technology.
actors.role: Co‑authored criticism of Commoner's work, contributing to the development and simplification of the IPAT equation.
actors.supporting_text: Ehrlich and his colleague John P. Holdren (b. 1944) accused Commoner of placing too great an emphasis on 'faulty technology' and of underplaying the role of population and affluence.

actors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
actors.description: U.S. Senator and political leader who publicly challenged the use of gross national product as a progress metric.
actors.role: Delivered a campaign speech in 1968 that highlighted the shortcomings of GNP and advocated for broader measures of societal wellbeing.
actors.supporting_text: In March 1968, Robert F. Kennedy (1925-68) delivered a campaign speech at the University of Kansas where he explained the shortcomings of using gross national product (GNP) to measure progress:

actors.name: Aurelio Peccei
actors.description: Industrialist who, together with Alexander King, convened an international group to discuss resource consumption.
actors.role: Co‑initiated the meeting in Rome that led to the founding of the Club of Rome, a focal point for concerns about global resource limits.
actors.supporting_text: In 1968, the industrialist Aurelio Peccei (1908-84) and Scottish scientist Alexander King (1909-2007) invited an international group of professionals from industry, academia and civil society to a villa in Rome.

actors.name: Alexander King
actors.description: Scottish scientist who co‑organized the 1968 Rome meeting on resource consumption.
actors.role: Co‑initiated the gathering that resulted in the creation of the Club of Rome.
actors.supporting_text: In 1968, the industrialist Aurelio Peccei (1908-84) and Scottish scientist Alexander King (1909-2007) invited an international group of professionals from industry, academia and civil society to a villa in Rome.

actors.name: Club of Rome
actors.description: International think‑tank founded in 1968 to study global limits to growth and resource consumption.
actors.role: Served as the institutional hub for research and advocacy on the interconnections between economic activity and environmental limits, publishing *The Limits to Growth* report.
actors.supporting_text: Following the meeting, the participants established the Club of Rome as a focal point for their shared concerns.

actors.name: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)
actors.description: Leading academic institution whose systems scientists developed the first integrated global model linking economy and environment.
actors.role: Provided the scientific and modeling foundation for *The Limits to Growth* report, linking population, production, pollution, and resource use.
actors.supporting_text: The Club's first report, The Limits to Growth (1972), was underpinned by the work of a group of systems scientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), who had developed the first integrated global model linking the world economy and the environment.

actors.name: Julian Simon
actors.description: Economist and academic who challenged the notion of physical limits to resources and argued for technological substitution.
actors.role: Publicly disputed the limits‑to‑growth perspective, authoring *The Ultimate Resource* and engaging in a high‑profile wager with Ehrlich on metal prices.
actors.supporting_text: Julian Simon (1932-98) was among the most prominent academics to challenge the idea that there are physical limits to resources that must ultimately constrain economic growth.

actors.name: Kenneth Boulding
actors.description: Economist who introduced the ‘spaceship Earth’ metaphor to illustrate resource limits.
actors.role: Helped make the resource limitations of the economic system understandable to the wider public, laying conceptual groundwork for ecological economics.
actors.supporting_text: Boulding's use of the spaceship Earth metaphor made the resource limitations of the economic system understandable to the wider public.

actors.name: Nicholas Georgescu‑Roegen
actors.description: Mathematical economist who applied thermodynamic principles to economic theory.
actors.role: Developed the entropy‑based critique of economic processes and later dedicated his career to a bio‑economic programme, influencing ecological economics.
actors.supporting_text: the mathematical economist Nicholas Georgescu‑Roegen (1906‑94) applied similar ideas to economic theory.

actors.name: Herman E. Daly
actors.description: Ecological economist known for the steady‑state economy concept.
actors.role: Observed Georgescu‑Roegen’s predictions and later articulated the steady‑state economy as an alternative to conventional growth paradigms.
actors.supporting_text: As Herman E. Daly (b. 1938) later observed, Georgescu‑Roegen predicted that the need for biofuels would place land for energy crops in competition with land for food.

actors.name: Ernst F. Schumacher
actors.description: Economist and author of *Small is Beautiful* who promoted appropriate technology.
actors.role: Championed the use of appropriate technology and argued that natural resources should be treated as capital, influencing ecological economics.
actors.supporting_text: This argument was shared by Ernst F. Schumacher (1911‑77), who championed the use of appropriate technology in Small is Beautiful: A Study of Economics as if People Mattered (1973).

actors.name: Robert Costanza
actors.description: Ecological economist who expanded the field after its early pioneers.
actors.role: Further developed the ideas of Georgescu‑Roegen, Boulding and Schumacher within ecological economics.
actors.supporting_text: Daly and Robert Costanza (b. 1950) further developed the ideas of their predecessors in ecological economics.

actors.name: Marilyn Waring
actors.description: Feminist economist critical of GDP as a measure of wellbeing.
actors.role: Highlighted the need for alternatives to GDP by exposing its methodological flaws and advocating for broader wellbeing metrics.
actors.supporting_text: In the 1980s, the need to provide alternatives to the gross domestic product (GDP) was highlighted by feminist economist Marilyn Waring (b. 1952), who criticised the GDP as a system which 'counts oil spills and wars as contributors to economic growth, while child-rearing and housekeeping are deemed valueless'.

actors.name: John B. Cobb
actors.description: Theologian and economist who co‑created an index of sustainable economic welfare.
actors.role: Constructed an index intended to replace GNP as a measure of economic wellbeing, linking economic and environmental performance.
actors.supporting_text: Following this, Daly and John B. Cobb (b. 1925) constructed an index of sustainable economic welfare intended to replace GNP as a measure of economic wellbeing.

actors.name: World Bank
actors.description: International financial institution that supports development projects worldwide.
actors.role: Launched a 2010 plan, backed by several governments, to create an accounting measure that places natural wealth alongside traditional financial metrics such as GDP.
actors.supporting_text: In 2010 the World Bank launched a plan, backed by India, Mexico and a number of other countries, to create an accounting measure that puts the natural wealth of nations alongside financial measurements such as GDP.

actors.name: India
actors.description: Sovereign state in South Asia.
actors.role: Supported the World Bank’s 2010 initiative to develop a natural‑wealth accounting framework.
actors.supporting_text: In 2010 the World Bank launched a plan, backed by India, Mexico and a number of other countries, to create an accounting measure that puts the natural wealth of nations alongside financial measurements such as GDP.

actors.name: Mexico
actors.description: Sovereign state in North America.
actors.role: Supported the World Bank’s 2010 initiative to develop a natural‑wealth accounting framework.
actors.supporting_text: In 2010 the World Bank launched a plan, backed by India, Mexico and a number of other countries, to create an accounting measure that puts the natural wealth of nations alongside financial measurements such as GDP.

actors.name: Beaver Committee
actors.description: A committee that conducted an early economic costing of air‑pollution damage in the mid‑1950s.
actors.role: Provided an early monetary estimate of environmental damage to support policy action on air pollution.
actors.supporting_text: An early attempt at costing the damage caused by air pollution was made by the Beaver Committee in the mid-1950s

actors.name: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
actors.description: U.S. federal agency responsible for environmental regulation and protection.
actors.role: Uses cost‑benefit analysis to evaluate environmental regulations and policies.
actors.supporting_text: Agencies responsible for environmental regulations such as the EPA in the USA have used cost-benefit analysis extensively

actors.name: Roskill Commission
actors.description: A UK government‑appointed commission that examined options for a third runway at London Heathrow in the early 1970s.
actors.role: Applied social cost‑benefit analysis to justify the location of a new runway, highlighting challenges of valuing environmental impacts.
actors.supporting_text: When the Roskill Commission proposed a location for a third runway in London in the early 1970s, it used social cost-benefit analysis to support its case.

actors.name: Nicholas Georgescu‑Roegen
actors.description: Romanian‑American economist known for his critique of applying pure economic methods to environmental policy.
actors.role: Criticised the reliance on price mechanisms for solving environmental problems, influencing ecological economics debates.
actors.supporting_text: Georgescu‑Roegen was among those who challenged this emphasis on using economic methods to solve environmental policy questions

actors.name: John Holdren
actors.description: American scientist and policy advisor who, together with Paul Ehrlich, promoted the concept of public service functions of the environment.
actors.role: Advocated for recognizing ecosystem functions as public services, shaping early ecosystem‑services discourse.
actors.supporting_text: Holdren and Ehrlich advocated this idea and in an article for American Scientist described the 'public service functions of the environment'.

actors.name: Paul Ehrlich
actors.description: American biologist and author who co‑advocated the public service functions of the environment with John Holdren.
actors.role: Co‑advocated the framing of ecosystem functions as public services, influencing later ecosystem‑services frameworks.
actors.supporting_text: Holdren and Ehrlich advocated this idea and in an article for American Scientist described the 'public service functions of the environment'.

actors.name: Robert Costanza
actors.description: Ecological economist who, with colleagues, produced a landmark valuation of global ecosystem services in the late 1980s.
actors.role: Estimated the monetary value of ecosystem services worldwide, providing a high‑profile quantification of nature’s economic contribution.
actors.supporting_text: However, in the late 1980s Robert Costanza and colleagues attempted to estimate the value of ecosystem services provided by the Earth's biosphere.

actors.name: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)
actors.description: Leading research university in the United States that produced an early report on environmental services in 1970.
actors.role: Generated one of the first systematic descriptions of environmental services, seeding the ecosystem‑services concept.
actors.supporting_text: An 1970 MIT report of the Study of Critical Environmental Problems, entitled Man's Impact on the Global Environment: Assessment and Recommendations for Action, described nine 'environmental services' that would decline if the functioning of ecosystems were damaged.

actors.name: Sir Nicholas Stern
actors.description: British economist and author of the 2006 Stern Review on the economics of climate change.
actors.role: Provided a high‑profile economic analysis that framed climate change as a massive market failure, influencing international debate and policy discussions on valuing nature and future generations.
actors.supporting_text: In his review of the economics of climate change, Sir Nicholas Stern (b. 1946) described climate change as 'market failure on the greatest scale the world has seen'. The 2006 Stern Review is the most high‑profile example of economic theory presenting the case for environmental action.

actors.name: William Nordhaus
actors.description: American economist known for his work on climate economics and discounting.
actors.role: Advanced an alternative economic perspective using higher discount rates, arguing that early climate action may be less cost‑effective, thereby shaping scholarly and policy debates on climate valuation.
actors.supporting_text: Some economists, such as William Nordhaus (b. 1941), use much higher discount rates that lead them to conclude that Stern's approach is inefficient because early action is more expensive than necessary.

actors.name: European Union
actors.description: Supranational political and economic union of European member states.
actors.role: Implemented a continent‑wide emissions trading scheme, creating a market mechanism to price carbon and incentivize reductions in greenhouse‑gas emissions.
actors.supporting_text: The EU has established an emissions trading scheme, and the Kyoto Protocol allows for the purchase of emissions‑reduction credits through the Clean Development Mechanism.

actors.name: United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)
actors.description: UN agency that coordinates global environmental assessments and policy guidance.
actors.role: Produced a 2010 report quantifying corporate environmental damage, highlighting the scale of ecological liabilities and informing calls for greater corporate accountability.
actors.supporting_text: In 2010, a UNEP report estimated that 3000 listed companies were responsible for US$2.15 trillion worth of environmental damage in 2008, equivalent to 7 per cent of their combined revenues.

actors.name: BP
actors.description: British multinational oil and gas company.
actors.role: Served as a high‑profile example of corporate ecological liability through the costly cleanup of the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, illustrating the financial impact of environmental damage.
actors.supporting_text: The costs incurred by the global oil and gas company BP in cleaning up the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico illustrate the real‑world economic impact of ecological liabilities.

actors.name: Garrett Hardin
actors.description: American ecologist and author of the ‘tragedy of the commons’ concept.
actors.role: Introduced a foundational theory on the over‑use of shared resources, shaping environmental discourse on common‑pool management and the need for collective governance.
actors.supporting_text: In 1967, Garrett Hardin (1915-2003) developed the notion of the 'tragedy of the commons' where he used the analogy of common grazing land to illustrate that sharing common resources leads to over‑use.

actors.name: Garrett Hardin
actors.description: American ecologist and author of the “Tragedy of the Commons” essay.
actors.role: His ideas have been used to support the privatisation of commonly owned resources, influencing debates on common‑pool resource governance.
actors.supporting_text: Hardin's ideas have been used to support the privatisation of commonly owned resources.

actors.name: Evo Morales
actors.description: Bolivian politician and indigenous peoples' leader who later became president of Bolivia.
actors.role: Led protests against water privatisation in Cochabamba, which contributed to a political upheaval and his electoral victory in 2003.
actors.supporting_text: When a privately run water company increased the price of water and sanitation in the Bolivian town of Cochabamba, this set in motion a chain of protests against privatisation and a political upheaval that swept the indigenous people's leader Evo Morales (b. 1959) to electoral victory in 2003.

actors.name: Elinor Ostrom
actors.description: Nobel‑Prize‑winning economist known for her work on the governance of common‑pool resources.
actors.role: Criticised Hardin’s arguments and advocated for durable, cooperative institutions governed by resource users themselves.
actors.supporting_text: The Nobel Prize-winning economist Elinor Ostrom (b. 1933) has argued that Hardin's work has been used to rationalise central government control of all common pool resources such as fisheries, groundwater basins and irrigation systems, and to paint a disempowering and pessimistic picture of the human prospect.

actors.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
actors.description: 32nd President of the United States (1933‑1945) who introduced the New Deal.
actors.role: Cited as a historical precedent for large‑scale economic stimulus programmes such as the Global Green New Deal.
actors.supporting_text: US President Franklin D. Roosevelt's (1882-1945) response to the 1929 Great Depression was a series of economic programmes called the New Deal, which focused on relief, recovery and reform.

concepts.supporting_text: The UK anti‑roads movement is an example of a single‑issue campaign that was supported by a wide range of groups from inside and outside the environmental movement. It emerged in the early 1990s with renewed public interest in the environment. ... A feature of many of the UK road protests was an alliance between local residents, established environmental groups and more radical environmental campaigners. Newly established non‑violent direct action groups such as Earth First! (a US import) and Reclaim the Streets organised, or were present at, many road protest camps.

concepts.name: Direct action
concepts.definition: A non‑violent tactic employed by activist groups that involves physically occupying, locking onto trees, digging tunnels, and otherwise disrupting target activities to raise the financial and reputational costs of large‑scale infrastructure projects.
concepts.supporting_text: By occupying and locking themselves to trees, digging tunnels and doing everything they could to disrupt road‑building operations, they developed a new public image of the modern environmentalist. They also showed that campaign groups with limited resources and few links to the political establishment could use direct action to damage the reputation and increase the financial costs of large‑scale infrastructure programmes over time.

concepts.name: Buy Nothing Day
concepts.definition: An anti‑consumerist day first launched in the USA in 1992 that encapsulated the ideals of the emerging countercultural movement.
concepts.supporting_text: The anti‑consumerist Buy Nothing Day, first launched in the USA in 1992, encapsulated the ideals of this countercultural movement.

concepts.name: global counterculture
concepts.definition: A worldwide anti‑establishment movement of the 1990s that incorporated environmental issues and was distrustful of global brands and multinational corporations.
concepts.supporting_text: In the 1990s, environmental issues once again become widely incorporated in a growing anti‑establishment movement that was distrustful of global brands and multinational corporations.

concepts.name: anti‑globalisation movement

concepts.supporting_text: The anti‑globalisation protests of the late 1990s had distinctive organisational features. They were loosely coordinated, involved a broad range of participants, and linked together a wide range of social, economic and environmental issues.

concepts.name: independent media centre
concepts.definition: A self‑organised media platform that allows anyone to upload news and reports from protest events, used notably during the 1989 WTO Seattle protests.
concepts.supporting_text: When activists established an independent media centre for anyone to upload news and reports from the 1989 WTO Seattle protests, the website received over a million hits over a couple of days.

concepts.name: anti‑roads movement

concepts.supporting_text: In 1998, veterans of the anti‑roads movement and Reclaim the Streets participated in the Global Street Party that coincided with the twenty‑fourth G8 summit in Birmingham in the UK.

concepts.name: Internet activism

concepts.name: Environmental movement

concepts.supporting_text: The professional campaign groups that are closely associated with the environmental movement provide some coordination, but also compete for attention, funding and support. concepts.name: Sustainable development

concepts.name: Wise Use Movement

concepts.supporting_text: The counter‑movement has taken many forms, including the Wise Use Movement and the Global Climate Coalition.

concepts.name: Global Climate Coalition

concepts.supporting_text: The counter‑movement has taken many forms, including the Wise Use Movement and the Global Climate Coalition.

concepts.supporting_text: The Act aims to enable the UK to make the transition to a low‑carbon economy.

concepts.supporting_text: the Noel Kempff project ... serves as an example of how well‑designed forest carbon projects can result in real, scientifically measurable and verifiable emissions reductions with important benefits for biodiversity and local communities.

concepts.supporting_text: The Bill is based on a 'cap-and-trade' system - a market-based mechanism that sets a cap on overall emissions and then requires companies in the energy and transport sectors to obtain emission allowances to emit greenhouse gases.

concepts.supporting_text: In the USA, the Interfaith Power and Light network has provided a religious response to climate change.

concepts.supporting_text: Avaaz, a web‑based campaign community, uses the model pioneered by MoveOn. It claims 3.3 million members across 192 countries, and campaigns on a wide range of social, economic and environmental issues, including climate change.

concepts.name: 350 campaign

concepts.name: Environmental movement

concepts.name: Anti‑consumerism counter‑culture

concepts.supporting_text: This chapter has examined the emergence of contemporary environmentalism as a new social movement from its early beginnings in nature conservation to the rise of a global anti‑consumerism counter‑culture.

concepts.name: Issue‑attention cycle

Over time, the public and the media lose interest, and the problem gradually fades from the public consciousness, often unresolved.

concepts.name: Green living

concepts.supporting_text: There are over 250 transition towns and cities, spanning twelve countries, working to raise awareness of green living.

concepts.name: Sustainable development
concepts.definition: Efforts to promote development that balances environmental protection with socio‑economic goals, with a particular emphasis on eradicating poverty as an overriding priority.

concepts.name: Sustainable development

concepts.name: Type II partnerships

concepts.name: Second‑generation environmental issues
concepts.definition: A broad category of environmental challenges that emerged after the 1980s, including ozone‑depleting substances, hazardous wastes, climate change, hazardous chemicals and pesticides, bio‑safety, and persistent organic pollutants.
concepts.supporting_text: From the late 1980s onwards, MEAs were established to address a wide range of second‑generation environmental issues, including ozone‑depleting substances (Vienna Convention, 1985; Montreal Protocol, 1987); hazardous wastes (Basel Convention, 1989); climate change (UNFCCC, 1992); hazardous chemicals and pesticides (Rotterdam Convention, 1998); bio‑safety (Cartagena Protocol, 2000); and persistent organic pollutants (Stockholm Convention, 2001).

concepts.name: Framework conventions
