concepts.name: ecological principles
concepts.definition: Principles derived from ecological ideas that can lead to varied conclusions about how society, the economy and the environment should interact.
concepts.supporting_text: Ecological ideas inform the language and belief systems of many environmentalists, though ecological principles can lead to very different conclusions about how society, the economy and the environment should interact.

concepts.name: evidence‑based environmental policies
concepts.definition: Environmental policies that are required to be grounded in scientific evidence, using the case for action backed by science.
concepts.supporting_text: It is now essential for environmental policies to be evidence‑based – the case for action backed by science.

concepts.name: Ecology
concepts.definition: The relations between organisms and their environment.
concepts.supporting_text: In the 1860s, Ernst Haeckel (1834-1919) introduced the term 'ecology' to describe the relations between organisms and their environment.

concepts.name: Land ethic
concepts.definition: An ethic that emphasizes harmony between humans, soils, water, plants and animals as a single community, judging actions as right when they preserve the integrity, beauty, and stability of the biotic community.
concepts.supporting_text: Leopold set out a land ethic that emphasised harmony between humans, soils, water, plants and animals as a single community. In A Sand County Almanac he wrote 'a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, beauty, and stability of the biotic community. It is wrong when it tends otherwise.'

concepts.name: Mutual aid
concepts.definition: The idea that cooperation rather than competition is central to societal prosperity and progress, illustrated by examples from the animal world.
concepts.supporting_text: In his book Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution (1902), he used examples from the animal world to show how cooperation rather than competition was central to societal prosperity and progress.

concepts.name: Malthusian principle
concepts.definition: The concept that population growth is mediated by limits to resources.
concepts.supporting_text: Thomas Malthus (1766-1834) set out how population growth was mediated by limits to resources.

concepts.name: Theory of evolution
concepts.definition: A scientific theory explaining the development and diversification of species over time.
concepts.supporting_text: Charles Darwin (1809-82) developed his theory of evolution.

concepts.name: Modern environmentalism
concepts.definition: A movement that emerged in the mid‑20th century, especially in the United States, driven by scientific concern over the widespread use of chemical pesticides and their broader ecological impacts, leading to public awareness, policy scrutiny, and research on toxic chemicals.
concepts.supporting_text: The increased use of chemical pesticides and the concern of scientists over their wider impacts were central to the development of modern environmentalism, particularly in the USA.

concepts.name: Radical ecology
concepts.definition: A politically revolutionary ecological perspective that combines anarchist political philosophy with ecology, arguing that human relationships with nature require improvements in social conditions and that reformist environmentalism perpetuates social and environmental crises.
concepts.supporting_text: Murray Bookchin (1921-2006) developed a more politically revolutionary approach, in which he combined anarchist political philosophy with ecology in books such as Post-Scarcity Anarchism (1970). Bookchin's radical ecology described how human relationships with nature depended on, indeed required, an improvement in social conditions.

concepts.name: Deep ecology
concepts.definition: A biocentric or Earth‑centred ecological philosophy that places intrinsic value on nature itself, putting nature first and humanity second.
concepts.supporting_text: This viewpoint is often described as 'deep ecology' - a term introduced in the early 1970s by the Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess (1912-2009). This biocentric or Earth‑centred approach has often been interpreted as putting nature first, humanity second.

concepts.name: Reformist approach (human‑centred ecological management)
concepts.definition: A human‑centred ecological approach that emphasizes rational management of the natural world to enable human prosperity, supporting environmental protection without questioning existing social and economic orders.
concepts.supporting_text: Some human‑centred approaches hold that rational ecological management of the natural world will enable humanity to prosper, so placing an emphasis on enlightened self‑interest. This 'reformist' approach supports the management of the natural environment without questioning the established ordering of society and economy.

concepts.name: Human‑centred approaches to ecology
concepts.definition: Ecological perspectives that prioritize human interests and view rational ecological management as a means to human prosperity, often aligning with enlightened self‑interest.
concepts.supporting_text: Some human‑centred approaches hold that rational ecological management of the natural world will enable humanity to prosper, so placing an emphasis on enlightened self‑interest.

concepts.name: Ecology as a philosophy
concepts.definition: The view that ecology is not merely a scientific discipline but a guiding philosophy for living, challenging modern societal assumptions and practices.
concepts.supporting_text: For Metcalfe and Goldsmith, ecology was not solely a field of science, it was a philosophy to live by, one that challenged the assumptions and practices of modern society.

concepts.name: Gaia hypothesis
concepts.definition: The idea that Earth can be considered as a single living system in which life unconsciously regulates the planetary environment to perpetuate its survival, viewing the atmosphere as an extension of life.
concepts.supporting_text: Lovelock took this further by suggesting that the Earth could be considered as a single living system and that life unconsciously regulated the planetary environment to perpetuate its survival.

concepts.name: biocentric approach to environmentalism
concepts.definition: An environmental perspective that places living organisms at the centre of value, recognizing that the Earth's atmosphere is chemically shaped by life and can be seen as an extension of life.
concepts.supporting_text: The US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) scientist James Lovelock (b. 1919) introduced a scientific twist to the biocentric approach to environmentalism when he developed his Gaia hypothesis during the 1970s.

concepts.name: global-scale environmental science
concepts.definition: A revolutionary branch of environmental science that employs worldwide observations (e.g., satellite remote sensing) and modelling to address planetary‑scale environmental issues, thereby influencing political agendas and policy.
concepts.supporting_text: In particular, a revolution in global-scale environmental science has pushed new environmental issues to the top of the political agenda.

concepts.name: Conservation biology
concepts.definition: A distinct field of science that emerged from the study of biodiversity and species extinction, focusing on the protection and management of biological diversity.
concepts.supporting_text: Conservation biology emerged from the study of biodiversity and species extinction as a field of science in its own right.

concepts.name: Biodiversity
concepts.definition: The variety of life on Earth, encompassing the multitude of species, ecosystems, and genetic variation, a term that entered common usage in the late 1980s.
concepts.supporting_text: The term 'biodiversity' came into use in the late 1980s, and by 1992 international momentum led to the adoption of the CBD.

concepts.name: Climate change
concepts.definition: Long‑term alterations in global climate patterns, driven by interactions among the oceans, atmosphere, sea ice and land surfaces, and recognized as a major environmental challenge.
concepts.supporting_text: The climate science community followed a similar pattern of development... This led to the development of models that used relationships between the oceans, atmosphere, sea ice and land surfaces to improve understanding of climate change over time.

concepts.name: Burden of proof
concepts.definition: The demand for ever‑greater levels of conclusive scientific evidence to support environmental action, determining which side of a policy debate must substantiate its claims.
concepts.supporting_text: Firstly, there is a demand for ever‑greater levels of conclusive evidence to support action (the burden of proof).

concepts.name: Science under fire
concepts.definition: Politically motivated abuse and misuse of scientific knowledge that erodes the authority and credibility of science in policy debates.
concepts.supporting_text: Secondly, there is politically motivated abuse and misuse of science, resulting in a decline in its authority (science under fire).

concepts.name: Acid rain
concepts.definition: An environmental problem caused by atmospheric deposition of acidic pollutants, which became a focal point of international debate in the 1970s and 1980s.
concepts.supporting_text: International debates over acid rain in the 1970s and 1980s ... exemplify the contrasting ways this scenario has played out.

concepts.name: Genetically modified (GM) food
concepts.definition: Food products whose genetic material has been altered through biotechnology, a subject of contentious scientific and policy debate in the 1990s and 2000s.
concepts.supporting_text: International debates over ... genetically modified (GM) food in the 1990s and 2000s, exemplify the contrasting ways this scenario has played out.

concepts.name: Climate models
concepts.definition: Computational representations that integrate relationships among oceans, atmosphere, sea ice and land surfaces to simulate and improve understanding of climate change dynamics.
concepts.supporting_text: This led to the development of models that used relationships between the oceans, atmosphere, sea ice and land surfaces to improve understanding of climate change over time.

concepts.name: Acid rain
concepts.definition: Rainfall containing sulphuric acid that damages vegetation, stone, bricks, and aquatic life, a problem traced back to the industrial revolution and linked to long‑range sulphur dioxide emissions.
concepts.supporting_text: The problem of acid rain can be traced back to the industrial revolution... When scientists in Scandinavia and North America started to express concern about the disappearance of fish from rivers and lakes in the late 1950s and 1960s, it was not immediately obvious that this was due to acid rain... Tracing the source of this acid rain was not only scientifically challenging but also controversial.

concepts.name: Green movement
concepts.definition: A vocal environmental activist movement that pressured governments, exemplified by public reaction in Germany to forest loss caused by sulphur‑dioxide emissions.
concepts.supporting_text: Germany, though a large emitter of sulphur dioxide, was stung into action by public reaction to the death of much loved national forests and an increasingly vocal green movement.

concepts.name: Standard of proof
concepts.definition: The level of evidentiary certainty demanded before attributing environmental damage to a specific source, described as being raised to an impossibly high level by industry representatives.
concepts.supporting_text: Others raised the standard of proof impossibly high: a US coal industry representative asked Canadian scientists to tell him which fish were dying in which lake as a consequence of a specific power plant.

concepts.name: Burden of proof
concepts.definition: The responsibility placed on other parties (e.g., neighboring countries) to demonstrate that they are causing environmental harm.
concepts.supporting_text: The British government also emphasised scientific uncertainty and placed the burden of proof on other countries:

concepts.name: Scientific uncertainty
concepts.definition: The state of incomplete or speculative knowledge about the causes and effects of environmental problems, used by governments to argue against immediate action.
concepts.supporting_text: The British government also emphasised scientific uncertainty and placed the burden of proof on other countries.

concepts.name: Air pollution
concepts.definition: The presence of harmful substances in the atmosphere, such as sulphur dioxide, that reached levels deemed intolerable and prompted public demand for regulatory action.
concepts.supporting_text: The resulting Beaver Committee Report (1954) concluded that levels of air pollution could no longer be tolerated but also observed that 'sulphur dioxide is one of the most harmful of all polluting agents'.

concepts.name: Precautionary principle
concepts.definition: A central tenet of European environmental policy that demands a high standard of certainty that a product will not impact the environment, placing the burden of proof on producers.
concepts.supporting_text: In Europe, the precautionary principle has become a central tenet of environmental policy applied to GM food products, and demands a high standard of certainty that they will not have an impact on the environment, placing the burden of proof on GM producers.

concepts.name: Substantial equivalence
concepts.definition: Scientific criteria introduced by the US FDA to assess how similar a new product is to existing ones, focusing on structural and content similarity rather than the fact that it is genetically modified.
concepts.supporting_text: Instead, the US Food and Drink Administration (FDA) introduced scientific criteria called substantial equivalence to identify how similar new products were to existing ones. In this case, the fact that a product was GM did not matter; what mattered was whether it was substantially different in structure and content.

concepts.name: Pseudo scientific concepts
concepts.definition: Concepts introduced by policymakers in situations of scientific uncertainty to support decisions, despite lacking robust scientific backing.
concepts.supporting_text: In circumstances of scientific uncertainty, policy makers introduce 'pseudo' scientific concepts to support their decisions.

concepts.name: Frankenfoods
concepts.definition: A colloquial term used in Europe to describe genetically modified foods that are perceived as unnatural or dangerous, reflecting high public concern.
concepts.supporting_text: In Europe concern over 'frankenfoods' was high following the 1990s 'mad-cow disease' crisis...

concepts.name: Acid rain
concepts.definition: A form of air pollution resulting from sulphur dioxide emissions that leads to the death of lakes and forests, prompting international policy agreements.
concepts.supporting_text: By the early 1980s, scientists and civil servants at the UK Department of the Environment were convinced that it was in Britain's interests to reduce sulphur dioxide emissions... It was not until 1986 that the British government finally accepted the link between British air pollution and Scandinavian acid rain. An air quality accord between Canada and the USA was signed in 1991...

concepts.name: Scientific authority
concepts.definition: The power and influence of scientific expertise to shape societal understanding of environmental issues, which can be exaggerated, dramatized, or oversimplified and is contested by various interest groups.
concepts.supporting_text: Scientific authority has driven societal understanding of the environment. This has been marked by the exaggeration, dramatisation and oversimplification of scientific evidence.

concepts.name: Trust in individuals and institutions
concepts.definition: The confidence placed by the public in people and organizations (including scientists, NGOs, governments, and media) that can become as important as, or more important than, the scientific evidence itself.
concepts.supporting_text: trust in individuals and institutions has become as important, if not more so, than the science itself.

concepts.name: Burden of proof
concepts.definition: The principle that the responsibility to provide evidence lies with those making a claim, emphasizing the need for more and better scientific evidence, while also being challenged by issues of trust.
concepts.supporting_text: Whereas the burden of proof placed an emphasis on more science and better scientific evidence, the question of trust challenges the authority of scientists themselves.

concepts.name: Environmental campaign groups
concepts.definition: Organised collectives that employ scientific expertise to diagnose environmental problems and use that evidence in legal actions, petitions, and public advocacy to influence policy and corporate behavior.
concepts.supporting_text: From the late 1960s onwards, professional campaign groups employed scientists to study and diagnose environmental problems, utilising the evidence in lawsuits, petitions to government and public campaigns.

concepts.name: Scientific consensus (IPCC reports)
concepts.definition: A consensus created through a carefully designed process where the scientific community and world governments agree on report conclusions sentence by sentence, intended to make climate science relevant, understandable and clear.
concepts.supporting_text: The process of developing IPCC reports was carefully designed to create ownership by the scientific community and by world governments, who agreed report conclusions sentence by sentence. ... this carefully produced consensus, each of the IPCC reports has been challenged.

concepts.name: Climate scepticism
concepts.definition: A stance that questions the levels of scientific certainty presented by IPCC publications, often invoking claims of procedural improprieties and challenging the evidence for anthropogenic climate change.
concepts.supporting_text: For much of the 1990s, the Global Climate Coalition, an American industrial grouping formed shortly after the IPCC, challenged the levels of scientific certainty set out in IPCC publications. ... Academics such as the American physicist Fred Singer (b. 1924) and the Danish statistician Bjørn Lomborg (b. 1965) added scientific authority to a continuous stream of challenges to climate science.

concepts.name: IPCC peer-review process
concepts.definition: The procedural system used by the IPCC to evaluate and incorporate scientific studies into its assessment reports, which was alleged to have been manipulated to exclude sceptical research.
concepts.supporting_text: The most controversial of the released emails from CRU dealt with the rejection of data requests from climate sceptics, and apparent manipulation of the IPCC peer-review process to exclude sceptical research.

concepts.name: Scientific authority on climate change
concepts.definition: The recognized credibility and influence of climate scientists and institutions such as the IPCC in shaping public and policy understanding of climate change, which has been contested by sceptics and media narratives.
concepts.supporting_text: Direct conflict broke out in 2006 when Exxon Mobil, the world's richest company and a member of the Global Climate Coalition, was challenged in an exchange of letters that became public with the Royal Society, the world's oldest scientific academy. ... the Daily Telegraph ... summarised the atmosphere of hostility, claiming nobody was listening to scientists any more and describing them as 'white-coated prima donnas and narcissists [...] pointy heads in lab coats [who] have reassumed the role of mad cranks'.

concepts.name: Public relations disaster (CRU email leak)
concepts.definition: The 2009 exposure of hacked emails from the Climatic Research Unit, which was widely reported in the media and led to a loss of confidence in climate science, described as a public relations disaster.
concepts.supporting_text: The challenge to climate science reached a new peak after approximately 1000 emails from the Climatic Research Unit (CRU) at the University of East Anglia (UEA) were hacked and posted on the internet in November 2009... This was a public relations disaster from which climate science is still recovering.

concepts.name: environmental economics
concepts.definition: A relatively undeveloped field that attempts to outline environmental constraints to the economic system and to move away from a focus on economic growth, while also developing ways of ensuring environmental interests are reflected in the market economy.
concepts.supporting_text: Over the past half‑century, the development of concepts and theories that recognise the economic value of the environment has become increasingly central to the environmental cause… Environmental economics is relatively undeveloped. … a series of academics have attempted to outline environmental constraints to the economic system and to move away from the focus on economic growth.

concepts.name: economic value of the environment
concepts.definition: The idea that the environment possesses economic value, a concept that has become increasingly central to the environmental cause and shapes policy‑maker decisions alongside scientific evidence.
concepts.supporting_text: Over the past half‑century, the development of concepts and theories that recognise the economic value of the environment has become increasingly central to the environmental cause.

concepts.name: environmental constraints to the economic system
concepts.definition: Constraints identified by scholars that limit or shape economic activity in order to protect environmental interests, used to move away from a growth‑centric economic perspective.
concepts.supporting_text: a series of academics have attempted to outline environmental constraints to the economic system and to move away from the focus on economic growth.

concepts.name: greener economic system
concepts.definition: An economic system that integrates environmental considerations and promotes sustainability, seen as an opportunity emerging from the ongoing global economic crisis.
concepts.supporting_text: Meanwhile, the ongoing global economic crisis has provided real opportunities for environmentalists to promote a greener economic system.

concepts.name: public trust in science
concepts.definition: The confidence that the public places in scientific evidence and its use by the environmental movement, which has been eroded and needs to be rebuilt to support effective campaigning.
concepts.supporting_text: The challenge for the environmental movement is to rebuild public trust in the way it uses science to support arguments in order to take action to address environmental issues.

concepts.name: environmental agenda
concepts.definition: The set of priorities and actions driven by scientific understanding of environmental problems and solutions, shaping policy and public opinion over the past fifty years.
concepts.supporting_text: Over the past fifty years, science has driven the environmental agenda, explaining the cause and impact of environmental problems and the implications they have for society as a whole.

concepts.name: Law of diminishing returns
concepts.definition: A principle in agriculture stating that there is a maximum point of land productivity that cannot be surpassed, implying that the amount of available land limits population and wealth.
concepts.supporting_text: Anne‑Robert‑Jacques Turgot (1727‑81) outlined a law of diminishing returns in agriculture, arguing that there was a maximum point of land productivity that was impossible to surpass.

concepts.name: Malthusian principle
concepts.definition: The idea that population growth, initially driven by surplus food production, will eventually be constrained by limits to productive land and a resultant shortage of food, putting society under permanent threat of starvation unless population expansion is limited.
concepts.supporting_text: An idea forcefully argued by Thomas Malthus (1766‑1834) … Malthus explained that population growth, driven initially by surplus food production, would eventually be constrained by limits to productive land and a resultant shortage of food.

concepts.name: Stationary state economy
concepts.definition: An economic vision in which unlimited economic growth is avoided, emphasizing the preservation of natural environments and warning against the exhaustive transformation of land and wildlife for human use.
concepts.supporting_text: John Stuart Mill … championed the 'stationary state economy' and warned against the drive for unlimited economic growth.

concepts.name: Negative externalities
concepts.definition: Detrimental effects of an activity that go unrecognised, for which government intervention is justified.
concepts.supporting_text: Arthur C. Pigou … argued that when the detrimental effects of an activity went unrecognised, then the government should intervene. He described these detrimental effects as negative externalities.

concepts.name: Land economics (economics of the environment)
concepts.definition: A field of study that treats land and environmental services as economic factors, emerging only with contemporary environmentalism after earlier economic thought focused mainly on labour and capital.
concepts.supporting_text: As a consequence, land economics, or economics of the environment, did not develop fully into a field of its own until the emergence of contemporary environmentalism.

concepts.name: Environmental economics
concepts.definition: A field of study that examines the economic impacts of environmental policies and the value of natural resources, rooted in early economic theories that later influenced environmental thought.
concepts.supporting_text: remain at the heart of environmental economics.

concepts.name: Economic growth
concepts.definition: The increase in the production of goods and services, historically equated with progress and driven by technological innovation.
concepts.supporting_text: the drive for economic growth became a dominant feature of the twentieth century.

concepts.name: Malthusian tradition
concepts.definition: A line of thought that emphasizes the risks of overpopulation and its potential to outstrip resource availability.
concepts.supporting_text: In the Malthusian tradition, many of these books focused on overpopulation.

concepts.name: Cowboy economy
concepts.definition: A metaphor for an open, unregulated economic system characterized by reckless, exploitative, romantic, and violent behaviour toward natural resources.
concepts.supporting_text: He called the open economy a 'cowboy' economy, symbolic of a cowboy's 'reckless, exploitative, romantic and violent behaviour'.

concepts.name: Spaceman economy
concepts.definition: A vision of a closed, sustainable economy in which Earth is treated as a single spaceship with limited resource reservoirs and a finite capacity to absorb pollution.
concepts.supporting_text: He saw the closed economy of the future as a 'spaceman' economy, where the Earth is a single spaceship with limited reservoirs of resources and capacity to deal with pollution.

concepts.name: Open economy (as used by Boulding)
concepts.definition: An economic model that assumes unlimited resources and an infinite assimilative capacity for waste, lacking constraints on growth.
concepts.supporting_text: open' economic system without finite resources and a limited assimilative capacity to absorb waste.

concepts.name: Closed economy (as used by Boulding)
concepts.definition: An economic model that recognises finite resource limits and a bounded capacity for waste assimilation, requiring sustainable management.
concepts.supporting_text: closed economy of the future

concepts.name: Population growth
concepts.definition: The increase in the number of people, highlighted as a major concern for planetary capacity and linked to environmental sustainability.
concepts.supporting_text: Ehrlich published The Population Bomb in 1968, and directly linked population growth to the Earth's capacity to sustain humankind.

concepts.name: IPAT equation
concepts.definition: A simple mathematical concept that expresses environmental impact (I) as the product of three major determinants: population (P), affluence (A), and technology (T).
concepts.supporting_text: The IPAT equation explained how environmental impacts (I) are a factor of three major determinants: population (P), affluence (A) and technology (T): I = P × A × T. This simple mathematical concept brought together Ehrlich, Commoner and Holdren's concerns about the prevailing focus on economic growth.

concepts.name: Limits to Growth
concepts.definition: A concept asserting that continued exponential growth in population, industrialization, pollution, food production, and resource depletion will reach planetary limits within a century, leading to a sudden and uncontrollable decline in both population and industrial capacity.
concepts.supporting_text: The Club's first report, The Limits to Growth (1972), was underpinned by the work of a group of systems scientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), who had developed the first integrated global model linking the world economy and the environment. ... If the present growth trends in world population, industrialization, pollution, food production, and resource depletion continue unchanged, the limits to growth on this planet will be reached sometime within the next one hundred years. The most probable result will be a rather sudden and uncontrollable decline in both population and industrial capacity.

concepts.name: spaceship Earth metaphor
concepts.definition: A metaphor used to make the resource limitations of the economic system understandable to the wider public.
concepts.supporting_text: Boulding's use of the spaceship Earth metaphor made the resource limitations of the economic system understandable to the wider public.

concepts.name: entropy law (as applied to economics)
concepts.definition: The principle that whenever energy is used, the amount of usable energy available to society declines, based on the second law of thermodynamics.
concepts.supporting_text: In The Entropy Law and the Economic Process (1971), Georgescu‑Roegen explained that whenever energy is used, the amount of usable energy available to society declines. This argument is based on the second law of thermodynamics...

concepts.name: bioeconomic programme
concepts.definition: An academic programme emphasizing the importance of viable technologies that can maintain economic activity over the long term without using irreplaceable resources.
concepts.supporting_text: Georgescu‑Roegen went on to dedicate his academic career to developing what he called a bioeconomic programme.

concepts.name: appropriate technology
concepts.definition: The use of technology that is suitable to scale and context, treating natural resources as capital rather than expandable income.
concepts.supporting_text: This argument was shared by Ernst F. Schumacher (1911‑77), who championed the use of appropriate technology in Small is Beautiful: A Study of Economics as if People Mattered (1973).

concepts.name: natural capital
concepts.definition: The concept that natural resources should be treated as capital, not as expandable income, implying they provide a dividend rather than being endlessly mined.
concepts.supporting_text: Like Georgescu‑Roegen, Schumacher argued that natural resources should be treated as capital, not expandable income.

concepts.name: steady‑state economy (SSE)
concepts.definition: An economic model defined as an economy with constant population and constant stock of capital, maintained by a low rate of throughput that stays within the regenerative and assimilative capacities of the ecosystem.
concepts.supporting_text: Daly is most strongly associated with his attempt to articulate an alternative approach to the conventional growth paradigm in the form of the steady‑state economy (SSE). ... following John Stuart Mill we might define a SSE as an economy with constant population and constant stock of capital, maintained by a low rate of throughput that is within the regenerative and assimilative capacities of the ecosystem.

concepts.name: sustainable economic welfare index
concepts.definition: An index constructed to replace GNP as a measure of economic wellbeing, intended to reflect sustainable economic welfare.
concepts.supporting_text: Daly and John B. Cobb (b. 1925) constructed an index of sustainable economic welfare intended to replace GNP as a measure of economic wellbeing.

concepts.name: ecological footprint
concepts.definition: A measure applied to national economies that quantifies the amount of biologically productive land and water area required to support a population’s consumption.
concepts.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint, genuine progress indicator and happy planet index have been applied to national economies...

concepts.name: genuine progress indicator
concepts.definition: An alternative metric to GDP that attempts to account for environmental and social factors in assessing economic progress.
concepts.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint, genuine progress indicator and happy planet index have been applied to national economies...

concepts.name: happy planet index
concepts.definition: An alternative indicator that combines well‑being, life expectancy and ecological footprint to assess national progress.
concepts.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint, genuine progress indicator and happy planet index have been applied to national economies...

concepts.name: sustainable development
concepts.definition: A broad idea linking economic progress with environmental stewardship, underpinning many alternative measures of economic wellbeing.
concepts.supporting_text: many linked to the idea of sustainable development.

concepts.name: Ecological economics
concepts.definition: A field that seeks to ensure the environment is recognised in standard economic theory and to set out an alternative to a capitalist (or communist) economic system by attributing monetary value to the environment and demonstrating the cost of its destruction.
concepts.supporting_text: Ecological economics is as much about ensuring the environment is recognised in standard economic theory as setting out an alternative to a capitalist (or communist) economic system. By attributing a monetary value to the environment and demonstrating the cost of its destruction, some economists have sought to reflect its value to society.

concepts.name: Cost‑benefit analysis
concepts.definition: A methodological tool widely used to make the case for environmental protection and to choose between different environmental protection options, though its application can be complex, controversial, and not always trusted by environmental campaigners or regulated industries.
concepts.supporting_text: Cost‑benefit analysis has been widely used to make the case for environmental protection and to choose between different environmental protection options. Agencies responsible for environmental regulations such as the EPA in the USA have used cost‑benefit analysis extensively, but its application can be complex and controversial and is not always trusted by environmental campaigners or regulated industries.

concepts.name: Social cost‑benefit analysis
concepts.definition: A variant of cost‑benefit analysis that incorporates social costs, used in policy proposals such as the Roskill Commission’s location study for a third runway in London, highlighting the difficulty of recognising multiple public values of the environment in economic terms.
concepts.supporting_text: When the Roskill Commission proposed a location for a third runway in London in the early 1970s, it used social cost‑benefit analysis to support its case. One of the most important issues to consider was noise pollution, but its application of cost measures to noise was widely challenged.

concepts.name: Ecosystem services
concepts.definition: A conceptual framework that relates the functioning of ecosystems to the provision of services for humanity, categorised into provisioning, regulating, cultural, and supporting services, and used to translate ecological functions into economic language that highlights their human utility and value.
concepts.supporting_text: An approach to communicating this in a structured way has its origins in the 1970s, when the functioning of ecosystems was related to the provision of services... Holdren and Ehrlich advocated this idea... The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment... defined the four categories of ecosystem services that contribute to human wellbeing as: provisioning services, such as food; regulating services, such as filtration of pollutants and flood control; cultural services, such as recreation; and supporting services, such as soil formation and photosynthesis... In the late 1980s Robert Costanza and colleagues attempted to estimate the value of ecosystem services provided by the Earth's biosphere.

concepts.name: Environmental services
concepts.definition: An early term describing nine 'environmental services' whose decline would follow damage to ecosystem functioning, forming a precursor to the modern ecosystem services concept.
key_proponents: MIT Study of Critical Environmental Problems
concepts.supporting_text: An 1970 MIT report of the Study of Critical Environmental Problems, entitled Man's Impact on the Global Environment: Assessment and Recommendations for Action, described nine 'environmental services' that would decline if the functioning of ecosystems were damaged.

concepts.name: Public service functions of the environment
concepts.definition: The idea that the environment provides public service functions, a framing used to argue for its protection and valuation.
concepts.supporting_text: Holdren and Ehrlich advocated this idea and in an article for American Scientist described the 'public service functions of the environment'.

concepts.name: Four categories of ecosystem services
concepts.definition: A classification within the ecosystem services framework that groups services into provisioning, regulating, cultural, and supporting categories, each contributing to human wellbeing.
concepts.supporting_text: It defined the four categories of ecosystem services that contribute to human wellbeing as: provisioning services, such as food; regulating services, such as filtration of pollutants and flood control; cultural services, such as recreation; and supporting services, such as soil formation and photosynthesis.

concepts.name: Market failure
concepts.definition: A situation where negative externalities are not recognised by the market system, leading to over‑use or degradation of environmental goods and requiring correction through policy instruments.
concepts.supporting_text: Following Pigou, these negative externalities should be regarded as market failures and corrected.

concepts.name: Negative externalities
concepts.definition: Costs imposed on third parties or the environment that are not reflected in market prices, causing the full cost of ecosystem degradation to be ignored.
concepts.supporting_text: Because many ecosystem services are not recognised in the market system, the full cost of their degradation is not considered.

concepts.name: Discount rate (in climate economics)

concepts.name: selling the sausage approach
concepts.definition: A marketing concept that focuses on promoting the desirable sounds and smells (the “sizzle”) rather than the product itself; applied to environmental issues, it is seen as failing to deliver the fundamental changes needed to stay within ecological limits.
concepts.supporting_text: In the 1940s, US salesman Elmer Wheeler advised businesses on his 'Don't sell the sausage, sell the sizzle!' marketing approach. Wheeler's secret to successful selling was not to advertise the sausage itself, but to focus on the desirable sounds and smells of the 'sizzle'... There is increasing recognition that the 'selling the sausage' approach to environmental issues is not delivering the fundamental changes required to stay within ecological limits.

concepts.name: value-action gap
concepts.definition: The inconsistency where individuals' positive attitudes toward green behaviour do not translate into actual environmentally friendly actions.
concepts.supporting_text: This inconsistent 'value-action' gap is where attitudes to green behaviour differ from actual behaviour.

concepts.name: green lifestyle
concepts.definition: A way of living that is perceived as environmentally friendly; however, there is widespread confusion about what constitutes a green lifestyle, with many people believing they already live green despite limited behavioural change.
concepts.supporting_text: This confusion about what a green lifestyle actually entails is evident in the responses to a 2009 UK survey on the issue. A green lifestyle was no longer seen as an alternative lifestyle by half of the respondents... the majority of respondents (61 per cent) felt it was worth doing environmentally friendly things... concepts.name: green heaven
